name: Layer 7 Cortical Interface
description: Layer 7 is a thin, flexible sheet of electrodes placed on the surface of the brain. The electrodes measure small voltage changes produced by nearby neural activity. Its surface position differs from an array of needles that penetrates the cortex. The sheet must work with recording electronics and other equipment; it is not a complete computer-control system by itself.

The immediate task to understand is cortical recording and monitoring around neurosurgical care. A high-density array can collect signals from many closely spaced locations, which may help researchers or clinicians study activity over the exposed cortex. Separately, the company aims to use cortical signals in an assistive brain-computer interface. That larger task also requires reliable decoding, a practical implant system and evidence that a person can use it over time.

For this coursework, choose the exact product before collecting a market size or business story. The temporary Layer 7-T electrode and a future long-term assistive BCI have different users, clinical evidence, costs and buyers. Treating them as one finished product would make all five sections difficult to support.
stage: A temporary electrode component has a 2025 FDA 510(k) record for use of less than 30 days. The company’s broader assistive BCI remains a separate investigational development. The clearest report would study the marketed component and explain the larger platform as its development context.
clinical_evidence: The reviewed FDA record, K242618 (2025), covers Layer 7-T cortical electrodes used with recording, monitoring and stimulation equipment for temporary use of less than 30 days. It does not establish approval of a permanent implant that restores computer control. The company separately describes the broader BCI system as investigational. This boundary changes the need, evidence and reimbursement sections.
summary: Interesting BCI technology, but first decide whether the report concerns the temporary electrode or the broader platform. Payment and exact-product IP are the main information gaps.
london_summary: No London Layer 7-T user was verified. The useful product-origin lead is overseas.

name: RNS System
description: The RNS System is an implanted treatment for selected people with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Electrodes are placed at or near one or two identified seizure sources. They connect to a neurostimulator implanted in the skull. The system records local brain electrical activity and looks for patterns that the treating team has programmed it to detect.

When a programmed pattern is detected, the device delivers a short electrical stimulation. This is the meaning of responsive or closed-loop treatment: the recorded signal affects when stimulation is delivered. It does not need to wait for a person to press a button. The clinician still sets and adjusts the detection and stimulation parameters; the device does not independently decide every aspect of epilepsy care.

Recorded data also give the clinical team a view of activity between appointments. This makes the product both a treatment and a source of long-term intracranial recordings. The case can therefore explain why sensing, stimulation, follow-up and data review have to work together. It should also explain the surgical and monitoring burden and the alternatives available to the same patients.
stage: This is a marketed US implant, with original PMA approval in 2013 and a substantial clinical history. The selected case should remain focal epilepsy. Investigational generalized-epilepsy work is a separate indication, not evidence that the original label covers every epilepsy type.
clinical_evidence: The original 2013 PMA concerns adults with drug-resistant focal/partial-onset seizures, with no more than two localized foci and other label criteria. In the 191-person randomized study, seizure frequency fell 37.9% with active stimulation versus 17.3% with sham during the blinded evaluation. The nine-year study reports a 75% median reduction, but that later figure comes from open-label follow-up, not another nine-year randomized comparison. A July 2026 company FDA update did not establish approval for generalized epilepsy.
summary: One of the clearer choices for public research: trials, an early patent, a detailed prospectus and an economic model are already identified. Early financing still needs careful extraction.
london_summary: No exact RNS user in London was verified. Use product-specific US evidence rather than presenting a general London epilepsy specialist as an RNS contact.

contacts.how_helpful: Useful for the early clinical need, trial design, regulatory development and how chronic recordings changed follow-up.

name: Rapid Response EEG / Clarity
description: Ceribell is a bedside EEG system designed to make a brain recording available quickly in emergency and intensive care settings. The clinical problem is that a patient may have seizures without obvious convulsions, while a conventional EEG setup and specialist review take time. A rapidly applied scalp headband and portable recorder provide an earlier view of electrical activity.

There are several parts to keep separate. The headband and recorder acquire EEG. The Brain Stethoscope feature converts aspects of the signal into sound. Clarity-family software analyses seizure-related patterns and can assist assessment of seizure burden. These features have different development and clearance histories; evidence for one version does not automatically establish the performance of another.

The useful entrepreneurship story is the whole hospital workflow: who can put the headband on, how quickly a usable recording becomes available, how a clinician interprets it, and when conventional EEG is still needed. Reduced coverage and software assistance do not make it a complete substitute for every conventional EEG examination. Faster recording also does not by itself prove better survival or lower costs; those require their own evidence.
stage: Ceribell is a commercial EEG platform. The selected FDA document, K223504, concerns a later Status Epilepticus Monitor configuration. A report should trace the first hardware and sound-based system separately from subsequent AI/software versions.
clinical_evidence: The DECIDE prospective observational study enrolled 181 critically ill patients and assessed workflow and physician decisions. It supports a rapid-access story, not a randomized mortality benefit. A separate 38-patient emergency-care pilot contained only one NCSE case: its nominal 100% sensitivity has a very wide confidence interval. K223504 reviews the Ceribell Status Epilepticus Monitor, so it should not be silently treated as the original headband clearance or every later Clarity version.
summary: Useful public clinical and economic sources exist. The task is to choose the hardware/software version and reconstruct its early licensing and funding history.
london_summary: No exact Ceribell user in London was verified. A general London EEG researcher is not enough to support a product-specific contact recommendation.

contacts.how_helpful: He is relevant to invention origin, the clinical problem and the assumptions behind the economic case—not simply to EEG in general.
contacts.limits: He has a commercial connection to the company. A developer’s account should be checked against patents, trials and payer records; it does not establish London use.

name: SAINT
description: SAINT combines individualized brain targeting with an intensive course of transcranial magnetic stimulation for depression. A functional MRI scan is used to help choose a cortical target for the individual patient. A stimulation coil is then positioned using the treatment system’s targeting/navigation process.

The coil produces changing magnetic fields that induce electrical activity in the brain. SAINT uses an accelerated intermittent theta-burst schedule: multiple sessions are delivered each day over five days, rather than spreading the whole course over many weeks. The commercial product therefore includes software, a targeting workflow and compatible stimulation/navigation hardware.

Personalized targeting and accelerated delivery are the main features to investigate. The scan informs where treatment is given; it is not a live EEG feedback loop that decides each pulse. The business case also depends on practical delivery: access to MRI, staff time across an intensive day, repeat or continuation treatment, and whether a payer covers the full pathway. A clinic offering generic accelerated TMS is not automatically using the licensed Magnus SAINT system.
stage: The Magnus system received FDA clearance in 2022, and manufacturer material records commercialization in 2024. It is beyond an academic prototype, but the early small trial and later clinical delivery should be distinguished. No exact licensed London delivery site was verified here.
clinical_evidence: K220177 cleared the Magnus Neuromodulation System with SAINT technology in 2022 for adults with major depressive disorder who had not improved satisfactorily with prior antidepressant medication in the current episode. The early double-blind trial randomized 29 participants (14 active, 15 sham). Its size and follow-up constrain generalization. Manufacturer comparisons with remission percentages from unrelated treatments do not substitute for a head-to-head randomized study.
summary: A relatively clear university-to-company IP story, strengthened by named patents. Local product access and a fully verified payment pathway are less straightforward.
london_summary: No licensed Magnus SAINT site in London was verified. A clinic’s use of accelerated TMS alone does not establish SAINT use.

name: Exablate Neuro
description: Exablate Neuro uses focused ultrasound to make a small, controlled lesion in a brain target involved in a movement disorder. An array around the head directs ultrasound energy through the skull. At the focus, sufficient energy produces heating and tissue ablation. There is no implanted stimulation generator left behind.

MRI is used to plan the target and monitor the treatment, including temperature changes. The team can assess symptoms and side effects during the procedure while adjusting the delivered energy. In essential-tremor treatment, the aim is to reduce disabling tremor by interrupting activity in a selected circuit. This is permanent lesion treatment, rather than reversible electrical stimulation or the non-ablative ultrasound approaches being researched elsewhere.

The practical case includes more than the ultrasound device. It depends on a suitable MRI facility, skull/patient eligibility, specialist staff, treatment time and follow-up. These requirements affect who can benefit and the cost per treated patient. Essential tremor provides a more manageable topic than combining every indication and later bilateral-treatment expansion into one case.
stage: The original US brain indication was approved in 2016 for selected medication-refractory essential-tremor patients. Exact ExAblate equipment is documented in a London clinical paper, and UCLH publishes a relevant service route. Later indications require their own records.
clinical_evidence: The original US PMA (2016) concerns unilateral thalamotomy for medication-refractory essential tremor in adults meeting its label criteria. Later Parkinson’s and bilateral indications are separate regulatory events. A 2025 UCL/NHNN methods paper explicitly reports ExAblate Neuro equipment in London, providing stronger local evidence than a generic focused-ultrasound service description.
summary: A clear clinical and UK-payment starting point with a direct London team. Early development funding remains a harder section.

name: MAGNETOM Terra 7T MRI
description: MAGNETOM Terra is a 7-tesla MRI scanner. It uses a strong magnetic field, radiofrequency excitation and receiver coils to produce MR images. It is an imaging platform rather than a neural electrode interface. Structural images can show anatomy in detail; functional MRI measures an indirect blood-oxygenation-related response rather than neuronal voltage.

A higher field can provide useful signal and spatial detail, but it does not automatically produce a better clinical decision for every patient. Field uniformity, RF exposure, coils, implants, movement and patient tolerability all affect usable scans. A good report needs one concrete use: what information does this scanner provide that the relevant alternative cannot provide as well, and does that information change care?

The commercial unit also depends on a building installation, trained physicists and radiographers, maintenance, scheduling and safety procedures. This makes the local facility team particularly valuable for understanding use and running costs. The difficulty is that the scanner emerged from a large company and a research ecosystem, so a simple start-up funding story may not exist in public form.
stage: The original 2017 FDA record concerns the 7T Terra system and specified head/extremity use, not every possible body region or later Terra.X feature. King’s lists an exact Terra at St Thomas’, giving a concrete installed-equipment lead.
clinical_evidence: K170840 records the original 2017 Class II clearance for the 7T system, including head and extremity imaging within its stated patient constraints. Do not extend that original label to every body region, all patients or newer Terra.X capabilities. King’s lists an exact MAGNETOM Terra at its LoCUS advanced MRI facility at St Thomas’, and a 2023 institutional report documents clinical/research use.
summary: A good local equipment discussion is plausible. Early IP and device-specific development finance are harder to reconstruct than the technical story.
london_summary: King’s lists the exact Terra scanner at the LoCUS facility in St Thomas’ Hospital and publishes a facility enquiry email.

contacts.limits: A facility operator may not know Siemens’ original R&D budget or patent history. Equipment proximity does not solve those sections.

name: Viz LVO
description: Viz LVO is software used in a stroke-care workflow. It analyses CT angiography images for findings suspicious for a large-vessel occlusion: a blockage in a major artery supplying the brain. It then helps notify the relevant team so that a potentially urgent scan can be reviewed and care coordinated more quickly.

The product is therefore doing a triage and communication task. It is not collecting a neural signal, replacing the CT scanner or independently making the final treatment decision. A clinician still needs to assess the images and the patient. The useful comparison is with the same hospital pathway before the automated alert: which hand-off or review delay could it remove?

The mechanism explains what the evidence must show. Image-detection accuracy is one question; whether the alert changes response time is another; whether that improves patient outcome or reduces costs is another. Hospital IT integration, the users receiving alerts and the institution paying for the software all belong in the commercialization story. The first FDA record used the name ContaCT, so product names need to be followed through the early history.
stage: The original 2018 De Novo authorization established a computer-aided triage/notification use. This is a marketed software lineage, but a report should follow the chosen Viz LVO version and avoid treating the whole present Viz platform as the original product.
clinical_evidence: The original 2018 FDA De Novo record, DEN170073, uses the name ContaCT and establishes the triage/notification category. The first authorization is a strong primary source for what the algorithm was allowed to do and how performance was evaluated. A complete case must connect diagnostic performance to time-to-treatment and patient outcomes without assuming that one proves the other.
summary: A clear software-regulation source and a relevant London co-founder. Original IP, early financing and a verified payer source need more work.

name: Optune Gio
description: Optune Gio is a portable treatment for glioblastoma that delivers alternating electric fields through arrays placed on the scalp. These Tumor Treating Fields are intended to interfere with processes involved in tumour-cell division. The treatment is aimed at the tumour; it is not measuring brain activity or trying to change neuronal firing as a neurostimulator would.

The patient wears and manages the system for long periods outside the hospital, with help from clinical and device-support staff. Scalp preparation, array changes, skin effects, carrying the equipment and sustaining daily use are therefore central to understanding the product. A report that only describes the electric-field mechanism would miss much of the real treatment and adoption problem.

The clinical setting also matters. The device history includes recurrent glioblastoma, a later newly diagnosed indication used with temozolomide after initial treatment, and changing product names. Those should be traced rather than combined as if they were a single first launch. Novocure’s devices for other cancers are separate topics, even when they use the same broad treatment principle.
stage: The lineage includes the original recurrent-disease device and a 2015 PMA supplement for newly diagnosed glioblastoma. Exact Optune clinical experience is documented at Imperial. UK private use and trial participation must be distinguished from routine NHS funding.
clinical_evidence: The product lineage matters: the original NovoTTF-100A recurrent-glioblastoma pathway, the 2015 PMA supplement for newly diagnosed glioblastoma with temozolomide after standard initial treatment, and the later Optune Gio branding should be traced separately. This brief concerns brain-tumour use; do not borrow indications for Novocure devices used in other cancers. FDA evidence and the company’s public prospectus provide an unusually substantial starting set.
summary: A strong starting point for the overall project: substantial public business/regulatory records and a London clinician with documented experience of the exact product.

name: Canvas Dx
description: Canvas Dx is a software-based aid for assessing autism in young children with developmental concerns. It combines information from a caregiver questionnaire, a healthcare professional questionnaire and short videos of the child’s behaviour. In the original FDA-described workflow, trained video analysts supplied observations used by the system; it should not be described simply as an autonomous AI that watches a video and gives a final diagnosis.

The system supports a clinician’s assessment and can return an indeterminate result. That possibility is part of the product’s design and clinical pathway: the report needs to explain what happens to children whom the tool cannot classify, not only quote accuracy for children who receive a definite answer. It measures behaviour rather than EEG, brain imaging or implanted neural signals.

The commercial problem is access to timely assessment and appropriate next steps. Useful investigation would ask whether it changes the time to a clinically useful decision, how clinicians and caregivers provide the required inputs, and who pays for the tool and professional work. Changes to software thresholds can alter how often a result is produced, so the original study and later versions must be kept separate.
stage: The original FDA De Novo authorization dates to 2021, and a later 510(k) software record is available. A Wyoming Medicaid provider bulletin documents a payment pathway effective in 2024. No London product user was verified.
clinical_evidence: The original 2021 De Novo record, DEN200069, covers children aged 18–72 months with potential developmental delay and use alongside professional assessment. Its original study included 425 children: 290 (68.24%) received no result. Sensitivity of 63/64 (98.44%) and specificity of 56/71 (78.87%) apply to the 135 determinate cases, not all 425. Those are historical-version results, not a benchmark for every later software threshold or population.
summary: There is more concrete payer information than the earlier comparison showed: an actual state Medicaid bulletin is available. Product-specific IP and London access remain harder.
london_summary: No Canvas Dx user in London was verified. A general autism researcher is not a substitute for a product developer or clinical user.

contacts.connection: Cognoa’s Canvas Dx research history identifies Wall as its founder and places the foundational research at Harvard.
contacts.how_helpful: Useful for the original clinical problem, development of the assessment inputs and the academic-to-company history.
contacts.limits: This does not establish an exact licence or independent patent claims, nor does it make him a London product user. Obtain documents to verify any origin account.
contacts.route: Use support@cognoa.com, the published general enquiry route, to request a product-development introduction; no direct introduction is held.

sections.found: The original FDA study and company development history describe the target children and assessment process.
sections.how_to_use: Explain the diagnostic-access problem and include the pathway for indeterminate results.
sections.missing: Independent population/wait-time/cost evidence and current-version clinical utility. Original determinate-case accuracy is not accuracy for every enrolled child.

sections.found: The academic starting point is described, but a Canvas-specific patent/licence map was not verified.
sections.how_to_use: Use the Harvard/company history to ask for the exact inventions, assignments and data rights.
sections.missing: Original inventor employment, independent claims and licence terms; do not import unrelated Cognoa therapeutic inventions.
sections.relationship: Origin account, not verified product-specific patent rights

sections.found: A 2017 release reports $11.6m from Morningside and more than $20m raised since founding.
sections.how_to_use: Put the early company financing next to clinical and regulatory development milestones.
sections.missing: Valuations, earliest funds and the amount attributable to Canvas rather than other company work.
sections.relationship: Early company round; not a product-only budget

sections.found: The original De Novo and later software 510(k) records are public.
sections.how_to_use: Explain intended use, safeguards and how the software lineage changed after the original study.
sections.missing: Other markets, specific standards/quality processes and the effect of each version change.

sections.found: Wyoming Medicaid’s 2024 bulletin assigns HCPCS A9291 to Autism Path 2 Care and identifies CPT 96112/96113 for professional assessment, with required documentation.
sections.how_to_use: Identify a real payer and who bills for the tool versus professional assessment.
sections.missing: Check current applicability, fees, other payers and health-economic evidence. This historical US state policy says nothing by itself about NHS access.
sections.relationship: Direct historical payer bulletin; not merely manufacturer advocacy
